item.title: Critical flaw affecting 70% of websites has cybersecurity world panicked
item.description: Emergency patches have been released for the vulnerability in PHP, which powers more than 70% of websites, as governments and operators warn of risks and urge developers to update systems ...
item.dc:creator: The Conversation
item.content:encoded: Details have been published of a critical flaw in the programming language PHP, which is the backbone of more than 70% of all websites. Left unfixed, the flaw would allow hackers to easily take over and compromise millions of websites and the information held on their servers. In response, multiple European governments and operators including the Port of Rotterdam have taken websites offline. The Australian Signals Directorate, America’s Cyber Defence Agency, and similar bodies from the United Kingdom, Europe and Japan have all warned web developers to apply urgent updates to their core systems, and to consider taking down websites until safety can be guaranteed.The organisation behind the free, open-source language has published updates that patch the flaw, but performing the updates on the millions of systems that use PHP will take time.What is PHP?PHP is often called “the backbone of the web”. It’s a programming language – a way to give instructions to computers – that has been around since 1997, and it allows websites to manage user inputs and process information behind the scenes.The power of PHP is its versatility. Websites use it for everything from logging users into accounts and running online stores, to requesting data from databases and powering millions of blog posts and news sites.PHP runs on the server rather than your personal computer. This means most of us interact with PHP every single day without ever seeing it.A timeline of concernsIn August, a cybersecurity researchers from a company called Wiz used their own tools and the latest versions of Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s ChatGPT AI models to trawl through PHP’s massive codebase.The Wiz team were searching for hidden programming weaknesses that an attacker could chain together to take over a system running PHP simply by sending a carefully crafted request over the internet.Within a few days, they found ways to break into PHP-powered systems from Drupal and WordPress which are used in huge swathes of the web.Wiz contacted the PHP security team to let them know about the flaws they had found. By late September, the PHP developers confirmed that the issue existed, and quietly began working on a fix.In cybersecurity, the responsible thing to do when you find a bug is to keep it private until a patch is ready. This is because public disclosure could provide a detailed map for hackers to exploit.This appears to be what the PHP developers were planning. However, yesterday a user on popular industry website Hacker News let news slip about the security flaws before any patches were ready.Following the leak, PHP’s developers rushed to publicly confirm the issue on October 21, releasing emergency patches ahead of schedule.Implementing the patches is far from simple. Because PHP sits underneath thousands of third-party plugins, frameworks and managed hosting services, websites are only secure once every individual layer of the supply chain integrates and deploys the PHP fix.Why does this keep happening?Much of the internet is built on foundational technologies that were developed and maintained by hobbyist developers. Many rely on goodwill and donations rather than robust corporate funding.Many of these tools were first developed decades ago. They were never designed to safely support a world where millions of websites and billions of devices use them to handle sensitive and private data.Compounding this issue is the fact that maintenance is rarely a priority for organisations. All too often, companies have only the most basic knowledge about all the pieces of their supply chains – either physical or digital.Even in high profile cases such as this one, many businesses don’t even realise what software they depend on, let alone have any idea of how secure it actually is.What should you do?This issue is mainly one for people who maintain websites or manage technical infrastructure. For those people, the priority is clear: patch systems immediately when updates are available, and consider taking down critical systems from the internet until you can be confident about their security.For everyday internet users, these vulnerabilities affect the servers hosting websites rather than your personal device. However, because some sites may be temporarily compromised before they can patch, it is wise to be cautious about entering sensitive personal data on unfamiliar websites over the next few days.Major cloud providers and security firms are rolling out emergency filters, but the global scramble to secure the web is just beginning.Cybersecurity teams around the world are rushing to contain the damage. But the scope of this issue should be a wake-up call.Governments and businesses cannot ignore the resilience of their digital supply chains. Just as manufacturers track the suppliers of the physical components they depend upon, we should expect that digital infrastructure also traces every system and framework it depends on.Gathering this information is the first step for businesses and governments to truly understand how heavily their digital viability relies on underfunded, volunteer-maintained code. Until businesses treat funding open-source foundational tools as a critical security investment rather than a charity, these vulnerabilities will keep happening.

item.title: Britain's migration clampdown puts fear into $20 billion care sector
item.description: Roughly one-third of workers in the UK's wider adult care sector are migrants, according to the Work Rights Centre ...
item.dc:creator: Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: By Lucy White In Britain, the government ensures that more than 650,000 vulnerable people receive daily visits from carers who help them wash, eat and attend to any medical conditions. That same government’s crackdown on immigration is putting the sector at risk. Roughly one-third of workers in the UK’s wider adult care sector are migrants, according to the Work Rights Centre. Around 280,000 came to the country under a Health and Care Visa between February 2022 and July 2025, a route that has since been suspended by the Labour government over fears it was being abused. Holders of the visas brought with them 429,200 dependents, many of whom also ended up working in the care sector. At the time the visa was suspended, Labour — under then-prime minister Keir Starmer — lagged far behind Nigel Farage’s far-right Reform UK in voter surveys. With migration high on voters’ concerns, the ruling party in September 2025 tasked a new home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, with introducing even greater restrictions on new arrivals as well as non-citizens already working in the UK. The government has signaled that, from July 2028, migrants will no longer be able to renew their Health and Care Visa, and instead will have to transfer to a Skilled Worker route. That carries a much higher salary requirement, and domiciliary care businesses — many of whom rely on contracts from local authorities — say they don’t get enough funding to cover paychecks of that scale.  “I will have to either downsize or just sell to a corporation,” said Shweta Maulayah, a managing director of a small care business called Maucare. “This is something that I built with passion, but I would not be able to financially keep it afloat.” The 2028 date looms large for many businesses and workers in the domiciliary care and supported living sector, which combined is worth around £15 billion ($20 billion), and their jitters are being heightened by Mahmood’s so-called “earned settlement” proposals.  Under current rules, a person arriving in Britain must stay for five years before they can apply for settlement, meaning most carers who came in 2022 and early 2023 would be eligible by the time the Health and Care Visa expires. But now Mahmood is proposing that the five-year baseline should be extended to 10 years, with reductions for high earners and those who make exceptional contributions to society through volunteering. Maulayah started recruiting from abroad in January 2023, and so has several staff who wouldn’t be eligible for settlement under those terms before the July 2028 visa deadline. “How am I going to keep them if it goes to 10 years?” she asked.Labour PoliticsPrime Minister Andy Burnham is leaning toward excluding care workers from the extension, according to a report in the Times newspaper, though it’s unclear whether the Home Office would support exemptions for people with Health and Care Visas.  Some Labour backbenchers object to the application of the new rules to people already in the country. Bloomberg reported in March that more than 100 parliamentarians signed a private letter urging the home secretary to rethink her plans. Left-leaning Labour lawmakers have made a set of demands, according to one person familiar with the matter, including that the new timelines for settlement shouldn’t be applied retroactively, that people from the same household should be able to benefit from the same timeline, and that the maximum timeline to claim settled status should be seven years. Cabinet ministers including Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and Housing Secretary Angela Rayner have also refused to publicly back Mahmood’s reforms. Mike Tapp, a former Home Office minister who worked with Mahmood on the proposals, has also called for an exemption for care workers. During Labour’s annual conference last month the home secretary gave a first hint that she was rethinking aspects of her reforms. “I know that, throughout our consultation process, some have said elements of these reforms are not fair,” she said. “We will come to a position that balances fairness for those who came here legally and fairness to British citizens across this country.” But that might come too late for some care firms. One owner of a domiciliary care business in the south of England, who was granted anonymity discussing commercial matters, said the uncertainty has prompted her to explore options to sell her firm or wind it up. Even if exemptions from Mahmood’s reforms were introduced for care workers, she worried that current restrictions on hiring workers from abroad ultimately made her business unsustainable, as she’d find it hard to hire British staff willing to work at the pay levels her contracts with the local authority allow. Maulayah faces the same dilemma. “We’re not getting a lot of locals joining this industry,” she said. “Even youngsters that go to career fairs, they’re not that interested because they feel that care is a low-skilled job. One of them said to me, ‘I’d rather stack shelves in Tesco,’” she said, referring to the Tesco Plc supermarket chain. Back in 2022, the industry was crying out for more staff. Thousands of workers from European Union countries had left the UK following Brexit, while its aging population meant there was relentless demand.  But, following an influx from countries such as India and Nigeria, it emerged that unscrupulous care agencies were abusing the sponsored visa route. A Bloomberg investigation last year revealed that many carers who entered the UK to work in good faith were being charged tens of thousands of pounds for their visa by the business who was supposed to be sponsoring them, but that there was no job for them when they arrived in the country.  Speaking to journalists on Friday, Burnham stopped short of committing to all of Mahmood’s proposals. “We’ve been consulting on those reforms, and we will come forward with our decisions soon,” the PM said. “But I strongly support the Home Secretary when she says that settlement is a right to be earned through contribution.” Proposals are expected next month. A spokesperson for the Home Office didn’t respond to requests from Bloomberg for comment.

item.title: Carlsberg India revenue slips to ₹8,708.8 cr in FY26, profit rises 22%
item.description: The company's total income, including other income, declined 2.25 per cent to ₹8,814.96 crore in the financial year ended March 2026 ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: IPO-bound brewer Carlsberg India has reported a 2.2 per cent decline in its revenue to ₹8,708.8 crore for FY26; however, its profit rose 22 per cent to ₹534.51 crore. The company's total income, including other income, declined 2.25 per cent to ₹8,814.96 crore in the financial year ended March 2026, according to financial data accessed through business intelligence platform Tofler. Carlsberg India Ltd, part of Danish brewing major Carlsberg Group, had reported revenue from operations of ₹8,906.50 crore and a profit of ₹437.94 crore in FY25. The company, which operates in India with popular beer brands such as Tuborg, Carlsberg Elephant and Kronenbourg 1664 Blanc, in July 2026 filed confidential papers with capital markets regulator SEBI for a proposed initial public offering (IPO) and received approval on October 1, 2026. It is preparing for a public listing, which, according to reports, could raise up to USD 700 million. Carlsberg India's royalty paid to its parent entity was up 13.23 per cent to ₹90.01 crore in FY26. Expenses on excise duty paid to governments declined by around 12 per cent in the financial year ended March 2026. It stood at ₹4,816.83 crore in FY26, compared with around ₹5,468.24 crore in the preceding financial year. Carlsberg India's 'Marketing and Publicity Expenses' were down 2.24 per cent to ₹69.22 crore. However, its expenses on 'Sales Promotion' were up 42.62 per cent to ₹848.71 crore compared with ₹595.07 crore in FY25. Total expenses for Carlsberg India were down 4 per cent to ₹8,090.81 crore in FY26. It was ₹8,426.23 crore in the financial year ended March 2025. South Asian Breweries Pte Ltd, Singapore, holds a 100 per cent stake in Carlsberg India Ltd. It is a subsidiary of Carlsberg South Asia Pte Ltd, which serves as the holding company for Carlsberg India.

item.content:encoded:
Home / Markets / News / Q2 results, US Fed decision, crude oil may drive stock markets this week

Q2 results, US Fed decision, crude oil may drive stock markets this week Besides, Jio Platforms' market debut, trading activity of foreign investors and global trends would also dictate investors' sentiment

In a holiday-shortened last week, the 30-share BSE Sensex tumbled 1,605.44 points, or 2.15 per cent, while the 50-share NSE Nifty slumped 546.15 points, or 2.36 per cent | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 25 2026 | 12:20 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Quarterly earnings, the US Fed interest rate decision, movement in crude oil and developments related to West Asia tensions will be the key divers for stock markets this week, analysts said.   Besides, Jio Platforms' market debut, trading activity of foreign investors and global trends would also dictate investors' sentiment, they added.   "Investors will track September industrial production and manufacturing output data on October 28. Corporate earnings will remain a key driver, with TVS Motor, Asian Paints, Trent, Sun Pharma, Bharat Electronics, Indian Oil, Bank of Baroda and GAIL India, among others, scheduled to announce their results," Ajit Mishra, SVP - Research, Religare Broking, said.

The US Federal Reserve's interest rate decision on Wednesday, October 28, will be the key global event, he said, adding that investors will closely examine the policy statement and accompanying commentary for signals on the future interest rate trajectory.   "Movements in US Treasury yields, crude oil prices, geopolitical developments and broader global risk appetite will also influence domestic market direction," Mishra added. "The US Federal Reserve's October 27-28 meeting will be the principal global trigger. Markets largely expect rates to remain unchanged, making the policy guidance more important than the decision itself. A continued focus on inflation could push US yields and the dollar higher and keep foreign flows into emerging markets under pressure, while balanced guidance may support a temporary recovery in global equities," Hariselvan Radhakrishnan, Founder & CEO of HST Wealth, a Research Analyst firm, said.

Domestically, industrial production data and quarterly earnings will determine whether India's resilient growth outlook can counter the external pressure, he said.   Meanwhile, Jio Platforms shares are scheduled to debut on the stock exchanges on October 28 and will be a key sentiment trigger for the primary market.   "Crude oil remains a central concern. Prices at elevated levels amid escalating geopolitical tensions threaten to push up India's energy import bill, complicate the inflation outlook and add pressure on the rupee and corporate margins.    The US Federal Reserve's upcoming monetary policy meeting will be another key event for global markets. Investors will look for signals on the interest rate outlook, particularly as elevated US Treasury yields continue to influence the dollar and global risk appetite," Ponmudi R, CEO - Enrich Money, an online trading and wealth tech firm, said.

In a holiday-shortened last week, the 30-share BSE Sensex tumbled 1,605.44 points, or 2.15 per cent, while the 50-share NSE Nifty slumped 546.15 points, or 2.36 per cent.
